targetQ.title: The target value
targetQ.context: With 20 requests a second as one instance's limit, what InvocationsPerInstance target does AWS's load-test formula give with its recommended starting safety factor?

choices.label: 600 a minute: 20 x 0.5 x 60
choices.feedback: Right. (MAX_RPS x SAFETY_FACTOR) x 60, starting with a safety factor of 0.5, leaves room for the time it takes to scale out.

choices.label: 1,200 a minute: 20 x 60, so no instance sits idle
choices.feedback: No. At the limit there is no headroom while new instances start, so latency breaks before scaling catches up. AWS suggests starting at a safety factor of 0.5.

plan.question: Before you run the week: which metric should drive scaling, with what target and limits, and why was CPU the wrong signal?

parts.label: The metric and the target
parts.criteria: Rejects CPU because the model saturates on concurrency at about 45% CPU; scales on InvocationsPerInstance at 600 (from the load test: 20 x 0.5 x 60) or on high-resolution ConcurrentRequestsPerModel for a sudden spike.
parts.modelAnswer: CPU never passes 45% when the workers are full, so a CPU policy never fires. Scale on what saturates: requests per instance at 600 a minute from the load test with a 0.5 safety factor, or concurrency per model, whose 10-second metric reacts fastest to an ad spike.

parts.label: Capacity and cost
parts.criteria: Raises the maximum to cover 120 requests a second (at least 6 instances at 20 each, more for headroom); keeps the CPU instance type within budget; pre-warms for a known event.
parts.modelAnswer: 120 requests a second needs at least 6 instances at the limit and 12 at the target, so the maximum goes to 12. Stay on ml.c5.xlarge: the GPU type is about seven times the price for little gain here. Raise the minimum before the ad starts, because scaling out always lags a spike.

expertPath.text: Flash-sale metrics: requests and concurrency rose, CPU stayed at 45%. Load test: 20 requests a second per instance. The ad: 120 a second.
Policy on high-resolution concurrency (or InvocationsPerInstance at 600), maximum 12, stay on ml.c5.xlarge.
Schedule the minimum to 6 around the ad and alarm on 5XX errors. The trade-off: about $4 of idle capacity for an ad that cannot wait for scaling.

outage.headline: Requests failed through the ad
outage.body: A CPU policy never fires on a model that saturates on concurrency at 45% CPU, and a maximum of 4 instances cannot carry 120 requests a second at 20 each. Scale on requests or concurrency, and size the maximum from the load test.

overBudget.headline: Fast, and far over budget
overBudget.body: The GPU instance costs about seven times as much for a model that gains little from it. Fix the scaling signal before buying bigger hardware.

fixed.headline: Scaled on the right signal, within budget
fixed.body: You read the evidence, scaled on a metric that tracks load, sized the maximum from the load test and stayed within budget. That is the expert path.

partly.headline: Through the ad, by a rougher route
partly.body: Check whether you load-tested before changing things, whether the target had headroom, and whether the maximum covered the peak.

scoring.modelReasoning: Scale on the resource that runs out first. This model's workers fill at about 45% CPU, so a 70% CPU policy never fires; latency rises only after saturation, so it reacts late. InvocationsPerInstance tracks load directly: AWS's load-test formula gives (20 x 0.5) x 60 = 600 a minute. ConcurrentRequestsPerModel at high resolution emits every 10 seconds and scales out fastest for a sudden spike. Size the maximum from the peak (120 / 20 = 6 at the limit, 12 at target) and pre-warm for a known event, because new instances take minutes. The GPU type costs $1.4084 an hour against $0.204 and adds little to this model.
